children: Fujifilm is turning India into a strategic manufacturing hub, Koji Wada, MD, Fujifilm India tells Urvi Shrivastav. Excerpts:

⁠India has evolved from being primarily a sales market for Fujifilm to becoming increasingly important for manufacturing, localisation and innovation. How has Fujifilm India’s growth journey changed over the past five years?

India has evolved from primarily serving the domestic market to becoming an important hub for manufacturing, localisation and technology. It is now part of Fujifilm’s long-term growth strategy, with expansion across healthcare, electronics, imaging and electronic materials. Our investment in semiconductor materials manufacturing in Dholera and the launch of endoscopy manufacturing in Jodhpur strengthen local capabilities. We are bringing global expertise to India while developing local supply chains, sourcing, talent and manufacturing. India’s market, industrial development and demand for advanced technologies are driving this transformation.
Which businesses offer the strongest growth opportunities over the next three to five years?

We see opportunities across our businesses, although growth drivers differ. Healthcare is important, supported by demand for advanced diagnostics, early disease detection and better access to quality care. We are strengthening our portfolio in diagnostic imaging, endoscopy and AI-enabled healthcare solutions. Semiconductor materials are another emerging opportunity as India develops its domestic manufacturing ecosystem. Imaging continues to evolve with consumer interest in photography and visual expression, while Business Innovation addresses changing enterprise needs. Our priority is to build on these opportunities and strengthen local capabilities.
What makes India strategically different from Fujifilm’s other major markets, and how significant could the country become within the group’s global business over the next decade?

India combines a large, growing domestic market with an ecosystem still developing across advanced industries. This creates opportunities in manufacturing, localisation and capability development. In semiconductors, India is at an early stage of building an ecosystem, and Fujifilm can support its development over time. We have seen similar journeys in Japan, Korea and Taiwan, where a strong supporting ecosystem was critical to industry growth. As capabilities mature, India’s domestic demand can become a strength. The country could become both a significant market for advanced technologies and a contributor to their manufacturing and supply chains.
Does the Rs 800-crore Dholera facility signal a shift towards manufacturing for India and beyond?

The Rs 800-crore investment in Dholera is an important step in strengthening our manufacturing and supply-chain presence. Our focus is broader than one customer or facility. Tata Electronics will be an important initial customer, but the expanding semiconductor ecosystem could create opportunities to serve other front-end and packaging companies.

Initially, some raw materials will be imported and processed at the facility; the longer-term objective is to source more from Indian manufacturers. Since the semiconductor-grade chemical ecosystem is still developing, this will take time. Fujifilm is open to supporting capable suppliers through training, technical know-how and, where appropriate, technology transfer.
What is driving healthcare demand in India?

The opportunity is not only about expanding access to technologies, but also improving how early and accurately diseases are detected, particularly as healthcare infrastructure grows beyond major metropolitan centres. Fujifilm is bringing global expertise in diagnostic imaging, AI-enabled solutions and endoscopy to address these needs while building local manufacturing capabilities. India needs technologies that improve the quality, efficiency and accessibility of care. We see scope to expand as the market develops, while adapting our technologies and solutions to India’s specific healthcare requirements.
What are the biggest constraints to sustaining growth, and how are you addressing them?

Developing the local ecosystem is essential. In areas such as semiconductors, specialised raw materials, suppliers and talent are still developing. We are working with local stakeholders and identifying companies with the capabilities and commitment to invest. Where appropriate, Fujifilm can support partners through training, technical know-how and technology transfer. Talent development is another focus, including opportunities to work with universities and provide practical, on-the-job training alongside experienced experts. Stronger local sourcing can help build a more resilient and competitive supply chain. These are long-term efforts, and capabilities will strengthen as the ecosystem matures.
Looking ahead, what does the next phase of Fujifilm India look like in terms of growth, investment and localisation? What are Fujifilm India’s priorities for the next three to five years?

Our ambition is to strengthen Fujifilm’s presence through business growth and capabilities that support India’s long-term development. The coming years will see us advance semiconductor materials manufacturing in Dholera, where production is currently targeted to begin in 2028, while expanding healthcare, imaging and Business Innovation. We want to deepen engagement with India’s industrial ecosystem by developing local talent, working with capable suppliers and bringing relevant global technologies to the market. For Fujifilm, growth must create value
beyond business performance, reflecting our Group purpose, “Giving our world more smiles.” We want our technologies and solutions to contribute meaningfully to customers, industries and communities.
